result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.predecessor()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- List every predecessor of each node on shortest paths from a source. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.predecessor()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- List every predecessor of each node on shortest paths from a source. title: >- [Graph.predecessor()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- List every predecessor of each node on shortest paths from a source. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} List every predecessor of each node on shortest paths from a source. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L53804-L53897){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.predecessor( source, weighted=None, cutoff=None, return_distances=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Shortest-path predecessors](/assets/graphs/predecessor.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A square of four nodes A, B, C, D searched from A (outlined). The arrows form the shortest-path DAG: A precedes B and D, one hop away, and C, two hops away, is reached equally fast through B or D, so C (accent color) has two predecessors. The card lists A: none, B: A, C: B and D, D: A." width="100%"} For every node reachable from `source`, returns the nodes that come immediately before it on *some* shortest path. When several shortest paths exist, all their predecessors are listed, so this dictionary encodes every shortest path at once (the shortest-path DAG). It is the building block for counting or enumerating shortest paths, for betweenness-style calculations, and for routing tables with equal-cost alternatives. The search adapts to the graph: breadth-first search on unweighted graphs, Dijkstra's algorithm with non-negative weights, and Bellman-Ford with negative weights (directed graphs only). ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The start node, as an ID or label. [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag. [cutoff]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional maximum distance; nodes farther away are left out. [return_distances]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, also return the distances. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, list[int]] or tuple]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : For every reached node ID, the list of its predecessor IDs (the source maps to an empty list). With `return_distances=True`, a `(predecessors, distances)` pair, the distances being `int` hops when unweighted. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the source does not exist, an undirected graph has a negative edge, or a negative cycle is reachable. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A node `u` is a predecessor of `v` when $d(u) + w(u, v) = d(v)$. Equal-cost ties are detected with exact floating-point comparison, as in NetworkX's `predecessor`, `dijkstra_predecessor_and_distance` and `bellman_ford_predecessor_and_distance`, whose results this method matches. Costs: $O(V + E)$ for BFS, $O(E \log V)$ for Dijkstra and $O(VE)$ for Bellman-Ford. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a square A-B-C-D, the node opposite A is reached by two shortest paths, so it has two predecessors: ::: {#0ec1c85a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec square = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) square.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "A")]) preds = square.predecessor("A") {square.get_label_from_id(n): [square.get_label_from_id(p) for p in ps] for n, ps in preds.items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'A': [], 'B': ['A'], 'C': ['B', 'D'], 'D': ['A']} ``` ::: :::
